meta.title: How an Ohio object takes shape
meta.summary: A little whistle, a curve in the clay—ooh, I want a closer look. Let’s meet the work behind a few Ohio objects.

recommendations.reason: I’m drawn to the glaze first. Then I want to know who made that curve. Come look a little closer at Cincinnati’s Rookwood Pottery.
Ooh, move a little—the light changed! Toledo’s glass story is one I’d happily linger over with you.
Ooh, a whole city behind an ordinary tire. Come follow Akron’s rubber story with me, from the workbench to the neighborhood.

blocks.text: Ooh, this little whistle has quite a voice. It began as flat brass, then someone cut, shaped, joined, and tested it. I’m fond of objects that surprise us when we look twice. Come follow this one with me, then we’ll see what a piece of clay becomes in Cincinnati. ♡

Turn a metal whistle over in your mind—or in your hand, if you have one nearby. Such a small opening for that much sound! American Whistle Corporation says it has made metal whistles in Columbus since 1956. Its process starts with brass sheet or coil, then cutting, forming, joining, and a final sound check. I’d follow those steps before peeking inside.

blocks.title: From brass stock to finished whistle

steps.title: Cut
steps.text: A press cuts flat blanks for the body and mouthpiece from brass stock.

steps.title: Form
steps.text: Tools bend the blanks into the curved shapes the whistle needs.

steps.title: Fit
steps.text: The mouthpiece and body are joined around the air passage, with a small pea set inside the chamber.

steps.title: Listen
steps.text: The company says finished whistles are tested by hand for sound.

blocks.caption: A pea whistle in section. Air passes through the mouthpiece; the moving pea changes its sound into a trill. Simplified, not to scale.

blocks.text: Inside a pea whistle, the moving sphere interrupts airflow and gives the sound its trill. I’m fond of that little surprise: a familiar signal has a tiny moving part behind it. Ooh, now I want to follow the whole cutaway.
blocks.title: Listen for the little sphere

blocks.text: Start at the mouthpiece and trace where the air goes. There’s the chamber, the opening, a seam, and a ring for carrying it. American Whistle explains that the moving sphere interrupts airflow in the chamber to make the trill. Ooh, the empty space matters too: the pea needs room to move. That’s the detail I’d miss if I only admired the shiny outside.

Sheet, cut, bend, join, test. I like how clearly those five actions let us follow the work. The company says it still uses original machinery and makes more than a million whistles a year. Curious about a tour? Its visit page lists them; check the current booking and access arrangements before planning around one.

Let’s turn to something quieter: clay in Cincinnati. Rookwood dates its beginning to 1880, when Maria Longworth Nichols Storer established a pottery in a former schoolhouse and potters worked with Ohio River clay. The company says each piece passes through at least thirteen sets of hands. Thirteen! That’s a lot of care behind a small thing on a shelf.

I’d start by following a curve on a vase. The clay has to keep that shape through drying, decoration, glazing, and firing; every stage changes what can happen next. Rookwood’s account makes room for patience and the little variations of handmade work. Look where glaze gathers or a maker leaves a mark. That’s where I tend to linger.
Designs shall be original, individuality shall be the goal.
blocks.attribution: Maria Longworth Nichols Storer, quoted by Rookwood Pottery

blocks.text: A useful vessel can hold an artist’s choices too. Rookwood’s history records a Paris Exposition gold medal within ten years of its 1880 founding; Cincinnati Public Library’s honors list dates it to 1889. The Cincinnati Art Museum also catalogs an 1882 vase. I’d look at that early piece beside the making story and see which details draw us back.

blocks.title: Follow the material across the state

blocks.text: Now I want to compare materials. Brass gives our breath a voice; glass makes me follow the light; rubber raises questions about flexibility and the road. The Toledo Museum’s account of its two 1962 glass workshops follows artists experimenting with studio furnaces. Akron’s rubber story takes us toward research and workers in the shops. Different questions, different hands to meet.

Pick one: whistle, glazed cup, glass vessel, or tire tread. What does its material need to withstand? What changes its shape? What does it let someone do? I’d look for the work that disappears into the finished surface. Tell me which object you chose—this is the sort of little conversation I could happily keep going.

items.label: In Cincinnati
items.text: Rookwood lists its working facility and showroom at 1920 Race Street. Its scheduled factory tours enter a live factory, require closed-toe shoes, and cover a large area. Confirm current availability and access arrangements directly.
